class/Accessory.d:
The Accessory Instance is the parent Instance of all accessories (regardless of their specific accessory type). It typically has a child Handle with a child Attachment and a WrapLayer in the case of Layered Clothing.

The Accessory class is the successor to the legacy Hat system. It's cross-compatible with both the legacy R6 character system and the new R15 character system.

If you insert an Attachment into the Accessory's Handle with the same name as an Attachment in one of the character's limbs, they connect and ignore properties inherited from the Accoutrement class. Otherwise, the Accessory functions identically to a Hat.

Note: If there are two matching Attachments, the resulting Weld is a child of the Accessory's Handle. This differs from the legacy behavior of Hats where the Weld is always a child of the Head of the character.
class/Accessory.s: An item that a Character can wear.

m.d: Specifies the AccessoryType of the Accessory. Is AccessoryType.Unknown unless you equip the Accessory through the player spawning process or Humanoid:ApplyDescriptionAsync(). If available on the Marketplace, you can set AccessoryType to categorize the Accessory item (for example, "Hat" or "Face").
m.s: Specifies the AccessoryType of the Accessory (eg. Hat, Tshirt, Waist).

kid.simple: What kind of accessory this is, like Hat, Hair, Face, Back or Waist. It's Unknown unless the accessory came from the player's avatar or a HumanoidDescription, or you set it yourself.
kid.example:
if accessory.AccessoryType == Enum.AccessoryType.Hat then
    print("It's a hat!")
end

kid.simple: An Accessory is an item a character wears, like a hat, hair, glasses, wings or a backpack. It holds a part named Handle with an Attachment inside. When added to a character, the Attachment snaps onto the matching Attachment on the body, like HatAttachment on the head.
kid.analogy: An Accessory is like a clip-on badge. The badge has a clip (the Attachment in its Handle), and the shirt has a matching spot (an Attachment on the body with the same name). Clip them together and it stays put.
whenToUse: Give a character a hat, sword on the back, wings, or other wearable item.
Check what kind of item something is (AccessoryType).
Remove or change what players are wearing.
kid.where: Inside a character Model when worn. Keep spare ones in ServerStorage and add them with `humanoid:AddAccessory(accessory)` from a server Script. Accessory inherits from Accoutrement.

terms.Handle: The Part inside the Accessory that you see. It's what gets attached to the body.
terms.Attachment: An invisible point on a part. The accessory's Attachment and the body's Attachment with the same name are joined together.
terms.weld: A connection that glues two parts together so they move as one.
terms.layered clothing: 3D clothes like jackets that wrap around the body. They use a WrapLayer inside the Handle.
terms.Enum.AccessoryType: The list of accessory kinds, like Hat, Hair, Face, Neck, Shoulder, Front, Back, Waist, and clothing types like Jacket.
terms.R6 / R15: The two kinds of Roblox character bodies (6 parts or 15 parts). Accessories work on both.

examples.title: Give every player a hat when they spawn
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (put an Accessory named PartyHat in ServerStorage)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ServerStorage = game:GetService("ServerStorage")
local hatTemplate = ServerStorage:WaitForChild("PartyHat")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    player.CharacterAppearanceLoaded:Connect(function(character)
        local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
        if humanoid then
            local hat = hatTemplate:Clone()
            humanoid:AddAccessory(hat) -- snaps HatAttachment to the head
        end
    end)
end)
explain: The PartyHat Accessory must have a Part named Handle, and inside the Handle an Attachment named HatAttachment.
AddAccessory looks for an Attachment on the body with the same name (the head has HatAttachment) and welds them together.
We wait for CharacterAppearanceLoaded so the player's own items are already on.
This runs on the server so everyone sees the hat.

examples.title: List what a character is wearing
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    player.CharacterAppearanceLoaded:Connect(function(character)
        local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
        for _, accessory in humanoid:GetAccessories() do
            print(accessory.Name .. " is a " .. accessory.AccessoryType.Name)
        end
    end)
end)
explain: GetAccessories returns every Accessory on the character.
AccessoryType tells you what kind it is, like Hat or Hair. .Name turns the Enum value into plain text.

gotchas: The Handle part must be named exactly `Handle`.
If the Attachment name in the Handle doesn't match any Attachment on the body, the accessory won't stay on.
Make the Handle not Anchored, or the character gets stuck.
AccessoryType is Unknown for accessories you add yourself, unless you set it.

class/Accoutrement.d:
An Accoutrement welds its child part called "Handle" to the player's character. You can change the position and rotation of the Handle part using the AttachmentPos, Right, Forward, and Up properties.

Parts descending from an accoutrement are massless when attach to other parts (e.g. with a Weld) as long as they are not the root part of the assembly that GetRootPart() returns. GetMass() returns 0 for parts in this case, and it doesn't add to the total mass or rotational inertia of the Assembly.

This doesn't apply to a part descending from an accoutrement when an accoutrement welds to another part that is massless or one if its parts otherwise becomes root. This also doesn't apply for the root part, and it has mass like a normal part.

class/Actor.d:
An Actor is a container for code that can be safely split into its own thread using task.desynchronize(). It should also contain the instances used by its scripts.

To learn more about using multiple Actors to optimize script performance, see Parallel Luau.

Notes

  • Each Actor runs in its own Luau VM. ModuleScripts required by an Actor are not shared or cached across Actors or with the main thread. Each VM executes its own copy of the module, so module-level state is isolated per Actor. Design accordingly if your modules hold state you intend to share.
  • script:GetActor() returns nil when called from a ModuleScript unless the ModuleScript is a descendant of the Actor. ModuleScripts stored elsewhere (for example, ReplicatedStorage) and required by an Actor are not considered descendants of the Actor.
class/Actor.s: An `Class.Actor` is a container for code that can be safely split into its own thread.

Note: Only the scripts which are descendants of an Actor may bind to its messages.

class/AdGui.d:
AdGui is a SurfaceGuiBase that renders immersive display ads onto a face of the Part it's adorned to. When no ad is available, it shows the creator-supplied AdGui.FallbackImage, or a default Roblox fallback image when that property is empty.

To render ads, the AdGui must be adorned to a block Part that's a descendant of Workspace, must be the only surface GUI on that face, and must be at least the minimum eligible size. When these conditions aren't met, the object displays a placeholder image in Studio's edit view and renders nothing in a running experience.
class/AdGui.s: A surface-based GUI that displays immersive ads on a face of a `Class.Part` in the 3D world.

It is the content-typed backing for AdGui.FallbackImage (a legacy TextureId string); writing to either property updates the same underlying storage. Unlike FallbackImage, this property accepts asset URIs and references to EditableImage objects. When empty, the AdGui renders a default Roblox fallback image instead.

class/AdPortal.d:
An AdPortal is an instance that must be parented to a Part — attempting to parent it elsewhere throws an error. When added to the data model, it registers itself with AdService to be served portal ads on rotation, and it uses a child AdGui to display the current ad's banner image and destination label above the portal.

When the local player's character touches the parent part, the portal teleports that player to the sponsored experience associated with the currently served ad. The portal only teleports while it is valid and has been served an ad with a destination place (see AdPortal.Status).
class/AdPortal.s: A portal that teleports players to a sponsored experience as part of immersive ads.

m.d:
Holds a human-readable explanation of why the AdPortal is not in a valid, servable state. When the portal passes validation the value is an empty string; when validation fails it is populated with the specific reason reported by the portal's validator, such as an unsuitable parent or a misconfigured child AdGui.

This property is read-only and defaults to an empty string (""). It is intended for surfacing configuration problems to creators in Studio.
m.s: A creator-facing message explaining why the portal is currently invalid, if it is.

m.d:
Reports the portal's current AdUnitStatus. The value is AdUnitStatus.Active only when the portal has passed validation and has been served an ad with a valid destination place; in every other case it is AdUnitStatus.Inactive.

A newly created portal reports AdUnitStatus.Inactive, because its destination place is unset (0) until the ad service fills the portal with an ad — the portal cannot become AdUnitStatus.Active, and therefore cannot teleport, until that happens. This property is read-only.
m.s: Indicates whether the portal is currently active and able to teleport players.

class/AirController.d: An AirController is a ControllerBase that a ControllerManager uses to drive a character's physics-based movement while it is airborne, such as while jumping or falling. While it is the manager's ActiveController, it keeps the character balanced upright, turns it toward the ControllerManager.FacingDirection, and moves it horizontally toward the ControllerManager.MovingDirection. Uprighting is tuned with BalanceMaxTorque and BalanceSpeed, turning with TurnMaxTorque and TurnSpeedFactor, and horizontal movement with MoveMaxForce. An AirController only functions when parented to a ControllerManager.
class/AirController.s: A physics character controller that governs movement while a character is airborne.

m.d: The maximum torque the character can use to remain balanced upright. When misaligned, this amount of torque is applied to reach the BalanceSpeed and realign the character. A higher torque means more force is required to cause the character to tilt. A lower torque means it's easer for the character to flip in the air. This property is hidden and has no effect when ControllerBase.BalanceRigidityEnabled is true.
m.s: The maximum torque the character can use to remain balanced upright.

m.d: The maximum angular speed used to align the character upright. A lower value means it takes longer for the character to recover to the upright position when misaligned. A higher value results in a quicker recovery.
m.s: The maximum angular speed used to align the character upright.

m.d: Determines whether angular momentum is preserved when input has stopped. If false, the character will apply TurningMaxTorque to bring the angular velocity toward 0 when there is no input.
m.s: Determines whether angular momentum is preserved when input has stopped.

m.d: Determines whether linear momentum is preserved when input has stopped. If false, the character will apply MoveMaxForce to bring the linear velocity towards 0 when there is no input.
m.s: Determines whether linear momentum is preserved when input has stopped.

m.d: The maximum force that can be applied on the ControllerManager.RootPart for moving in the ControllerManager.MovingDirection. This affects how quickly different target linear velocities are reached and how quick the linear acceleration is if MaintainLinearMomentum is off.
m.s: The maximum force that can be applied on the `Class.ControllerManager.RootPart` for moving in the `Class.ControllerManager.MovingDirection`.

m.d: The maximum torque that can be applied on the ControllerManager.RootPart for turning towards the ControllerManager.FacingDirection. This effects how quickly different target angular velocities are reached and how quick angular deceleration is if MaintainAngularMomentum is off.
m.s: The maximum torque that can be applied on the `Class.ControllerManager.RootPart` for turning towards the `Class.ControllerManager.FacingDirection`.

m.d: The value multiplied by the ControllerManager.BaseTurnSpeed to determine the final target angular velocity while this controller is active. The angular velocity is applied when turning towards the ControllerManager.FacingDirection.

class/AlignOrientation.d:
The AlignOrientation constraint applies torque to align two attachments, or to align one attachment with a goal orientation. As indicated by the name, it only affects the orientation of the attachments, not their position (to align attachments positionally, see AlignPosition).

Torque created by AlignOrientation is applied about the center of mass of the parent of the attachments, or the center of mass of parts rigidly connected to the parents.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Affected Axes

The axes affected by torque are controlled through the constraint's AlignType property. When set to PrimaryAxisParallel, PrimaryAxisPerpendicular or PrimaryAxisLookAt, torque will only occur when the primary axes become misaligned. Otherwise, the constraint will apply torque about all 3 axes to achieve alignment.

Reactionary Torque

By default, the constraint only applies torque to Attachment0 while Attachment1 remains unaffected. If desired, torque can be applied to both attachments in equal and opposite directions by enabling ReactionTorqueEnabled.

Torque Magnitude

You can configure this constraint to apply the maximum torque that constraints allow through the RigidityEnabled property. When true, the physics solver reacts as quickly as possible to complete the alignment. When false, the torque is determined by MaxTorque, MaxAngularVelocity, and Responsiveness.

Attachment Mode

This constraint can use either one or two attachments in calculating its goal. See Mode for details.
class/AlignOrientation.s: Constraint which applies torque to align two attachments, or to align one attachment with a goal orientation.

m.d: Specifies the desired relationship between the primary axes of Attachment0 and the goal. Available options are AllAxes, PrimaryAxisParallel, PrimaryAxisPerpendicular, and PrimaryAxisLookAt. The constraint will attempt to maintain the specified relationship, as given by the AlignType, by applying torques onto the relevant axes.
m.s: The constraint's axis alignment type.

kid.simple: How the part should line up with the goal: AllAxes (match the full rotation exactly), PrimaryAxisParallel (main arrows point the same way, free to roll around it), PrimaryAxisPerpendicular (main arrows at a right angle), or PrimaryAxisLookAt (point the main arrow at LookAtPosition).
kid.example: workspace.Turret.AlignOrientation.AlignType = Enum.AlignType.PrimaryAxisParallel

m.d: The CFrame orientation (translation component ignored) with which the constraint will attempt to match the orientation of Attachment0. Only used when Mode is set to OneAttachment.
m.s: The `Datatype.CFrame` orientation with which the constraint will attempt to match the orientation of `Class.Constraint.Attachment0|Attachment0`.

kid.simple: The goal rotation, when Mode is OneAttachment. Only the rotation part is used; the position inside the CFrame is ignored.
kid.example: workspace.Board.AlignOrientation.CFrame = CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(45), 0) -- face 45 degrees

m.d: A Vector3 world space location toward which the primary axis will attempt to align. This is only active when AlignType is set to PrimaryAxisLookAt and Mode is set to OneAttachment.
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector3` world space location toward which the primary axis will attempt to align.

kid.simple: A spot in the world for the main arrow to point at. Only used when AlignType is PrimaryAxisLookAt and Mode is OneAttachment. Not copied to players' devices automatically (not replicated).
kid.example:
local turn = workspace.Turret.AlignOrientation
turn.Mode = Enum.OrientationAlignmentMode.OneAttachment
turn.AlignType = Enum.AlignType.PrimaryAxisLookAt
turn.LookAtPosition = Vector3.new(0, 5, 50) -- aim at this spot

m.d:
Maximum angular velocity the constraint can use to reach its goal. Only used if RigidityEnabled is false.

Note that MaxAngularVelocity, as well as MaxTorque, are caps to the angular velocity and torque respectively. The actual scale is determined by Responsiveness.
m.s: Maximum angular velocity the constraint can use to reach its goal.

kid.simple: The fastest it may spin (radians per second) while turning to the goal, when RigidityEnabled is false. A cap, not the exact speed.
kid.example: workspace.Turret.AlignOrientation.MaxAngularVelocity = math.pi -- at most half a turn per second

m.d:
Maximum torque the constraint can use to reach its goal. Only used if RigidityEnabled is false.

Note that MaxTorque, as well as MaxAngularVelocity, are caps to the torque and angular velocity respectively. The actual scale is determined by Responsiveness.
m.s: Maximum torque the constraint can use to reach its goal.

kid.simple: The most twisting strength it may use, when RigidityEnabled is false. A cap; Responsiveness decides how much is really used.
kid.example: workspace.Turret.AlignOrientation.MaxTorque = 50000

m.d:
Whether the constraint uses one or two attachments in calculating its goal. By default, this is TwoAttachment, meaning that the constraint attempts to match the orientation of Attachment0 with the orientation of Attachment1, disregarding CFrame, PrimaryAxis, and SecondaryAxis.

If set to OneAttachment, the constraint disregards Attachment1 and attempts to match the orientation of Attachment0 with the orientation of CFrame, or match the attachment's Axis and SecondaryAxis with the constraint's PrimaryAxis and SecondaryAxis properties respectively.
m.s: Whether the constraint uses one or two attachments in calculating its goal.

kid.simple: TwoAttachment (default): turn Attachment0 to match Attachment1's direction. OneAttachment: ignore Attachment1 and match the CFrame (or PrimaryAxis/SecondaryAxis) property instead.
kid.example: workspace.Board.AlignOrientation.Mode = Enum.OrientationAlignmentMode.OneAttachment

m.d: The direction of the goal's X axis, represented as a unit Vector3. Only used when Mode is OneAttachment.
m.s: The direction of the goal's **X** axis, represented as a unit `Datatype.Vector3`.

kid.simple: In OneAttachment mode, the direction the goal's main (X) arrow should point, as a length-1 Vector3. Not replicated.

terms.torque: A twisting push that makes things spin, like turning a doorknob or a steering wheel. Torque = force x distance from the spinning point, so pushing farther from the center twists harder.
terms.angular velocity: How fast something spins, and around which axis, measured in radians per second. 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians per second is one full turn every second.
terms.radians: Another way to measure angles. A full circle is 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians, which is 360 degrees. `math.rad(90)` turns 90 degrees into radians.
terms.CFrame: A position plus a rotation in one value. It says where something is and which way it faces.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) bundled together. Used for positions, directions, forces and speeds. Y is up.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.center of mass: The balance point of an object. Pushing exactly through it moves the object without spinning it; pushing off to the side also makes it spin.
terms.world space: Directions measured using the whole game world's fixed arrows: Y is always straight up toward the sky, no matter how a part is turned.
terms.Responsiveness: How quickly an Align constraint tries to reach its goal, from 5 (slow and gentle) to 200 (fast and snappy).
terms.axis: An imaginary line something turns around or slides along. An attachment's X axis is its main arrow.
terms.deprecated: Old and replaced by something better. It may still work, but you should not use it in new games.
terms.replicate: Copy from the server to every player's computer automatically. A property marked 'not replicated' is not copied.
terms.orientation: Which way something is turned or facing.
terms.primary axis: An attachment's main arrow (its X direction). The secondary axis is its Y direction.
terms.AlignType: Picks how strict the turning is: AllAxes (match the full rotation), PrimaryAxisParallel (only make the main arrows point the same way), PrimaryAxisPerpendicular (make them point at right angles), PrimaryAxisLookAt (point the main arrow at a spot).
terms.MaxTorque: The most twisting strength it may use to turn the part.
terms.MaxAngularVelocity: The fastest it may spin (radians per second) while turning toward the goal.

examples.title: Turn a floating part to face a new direction
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 2)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Anchored = false
part.Parent = workspace

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

-- Keep it floating in place
local hold = Instance.new("AlignPosition")
hold.Attachment0 = attachment
hold.Mode = Enum.PositionAlignmentMode.OneAttachment
hold.Position = part.Position
hold.MaxForce = 100000
hold.Parent = part

local turn = Instance.new("AlignOrientation")
turn.Attachment0 = attachment
turn.Mode = Enum.OrientationAlignmentMode.OneAttachment
turn.Responsiveness = 15
turn.MaxTorque = 100000
turn.Parent = part

-- Every 2 seconds, turn another 90 degrees around the up axis
local angle = 0
while true do
	angle += 90
	turn.CFrame = CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(angle), 0)
	task.wait(2)
end
explain: AlignPosition holds the part in the air; AlignOrientation only handles the turning.
In OneAttachment mode, the goal rotation comes from the CFrame property. Only its rotation is used; its position is ignored.
CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(90), 0) means 'turned 90 degrees around Y'. math.rad converts degrees to radians.
Each loop adds 90 degrees, so the part smoothly turns a quarter turn every 2 seconds.

gotchas: CFrame, PrimaryAxis, SecondaryAxis and LookAtPosition only matter when Mode is OneAttachment.
If the part turns too slowly or not at all, raise MaxTorque (or Responsiveness).
AlignOrientation does not hold a part up. A loose part will still fall unless something else holds it.
Angles in CFrame.Angles are radians. Use math.rad(degrees).

class/AlignPosition.d:
The AlignPosition constraint applies force to move two attachments together, or to move one attachment to a goal position. As indicated by the name, it only affects the position of the attachments, not their orientation (to align attachments by orientation, see AlignOrientation).

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Force Location

By default, force is applied to the parent of Attachment0 at that attachment's location, meaning that if the parent's center of mass is not aligned with the direction of the force, torque will be applied as well as force. Alternatively, force can be applied to the parents' center of mass by toggling on ApplyAtCenterOfMass.

Reactionary Force

By default, the constraint only applies force to Attachment0 while Attachment1 remains unaffected. If desired, force can be applied to both attachments in equal and opposite directions by enabling ReactionForceEnabled.

Force Limits

You can configure this constraint to apply the maximum force that constraints allow through the RigidityEnabled property. When true, the physics solver reacts as quickly as possible to complete the alignment. When false, the force applied by the constraint is limited based on ForceLimitMode, MaxVelocity, and Responsiveness. See ForceLimitMode for further details.

Attachment Mode

This constraint can use either one or two attachments in calculating its goal. See Mode for details.
class/AlignPosition.s: Constraint which applies force to move two attachments together, or to move one attachment to a goal position.

m.d: When false (default), force is applied to the parent of Attachment0 at that attachment's location, meaning that if the parent's center of mass is not aligned with the direction of the force, torque will be applied as well as force. When true, force is applied at the parents' center of mass.
m.s: Whether force is applied to the parent of `Class.Constraint.Attachment0|Attachment0` at that attachment's location, or at the parents' center of mass.

kid.simple: If false (default), the push happens at Attachment0's spot, which can also make the part twist. If true, the push goes through the part's balance point, so it moves without tumbling.

m.d: Determines how the constraint force will be limited when RigidityEnabled is false. When set to Magnitude, the constraint force will be limited such that the magnitude is less than MaxForce. When set to PerAxis, the constraint force along each axis will be limited by MaxAxesForce. The axes along which the force will be limited are based on the ForceRelativeTo property.
m.s: Determines how the constraint force will be limited. Only used if `Class.AlignPosition.RigidityEnabled|RigidityEnabled` is `false`.

kid.simple: How the force is capped when RigidityEnabled is false. Magnitude: one cap (MaxForce) for the total push. PerAxis: separate caps for X, Y and Z (MaxAxesForce).

local align = workspace.Drone.AlignPosition
align.ForceLimitMode = Enum.ForceLimitMode.PerAxis
align.MaxAxesForce = Vector3.new(2000, 50000, 2000) -- strong lift, gentle sideways

m.d: Determines the axes that the constraint uses to limit the force. Only applies when RigidityEnabled is false and AlignPosition.ForceLimitMode is PerAxis. When set to World, the constraint force is computed in the world reference frame and the force limits specified in MaxAxesForce refer to the axes of the world coordinate system. When set to Attachment0 or Attachment1, the force limits specified in MaxAxesForce refer to the axes of the specified attachment coordinate system.
m.s: Determines the axes that the constraint uses to limit the force. Only applies when `Class.AlignPosition.RigidityEnabled|RigidityEnabled` is `false` and `Class.AlignPosition.ForceLimitMode` is `Enum.ForceLimitMode|PerAxis`. .

m.s: Maximum force along each axis that the constraint can apply to achieve its goal.

kid.simple: With PerAxis limits on, the most force allowed in each direction, as a Vector3.
kid.example: workspace.Drone.AlignPosition.MaxAxesForce = Vector3.new(1000, 30000, 1000)

m.d:
Maximum force magnitude the constraint can apply to achieve its goal. Only used if RigidityEnabled is false and ForceLimitMode is Magnitude.

Note that MaxForce, as well as MaxVelocity, are caps to the force and velocity respectively. The actual scale is determined by Responsiveness.
m.s: Maximum force magnitude the constraint can apply to achieve its goal.

kid.simple: The most total force used to reach the goal (when RigidityEnabled is false and ForceLimitMode is Magnitude). It is a cap; Responsiveness decides how much is actually used.

local part = workspace.Drone
-- 10 times the part's weight: plenty to lift it

Note that MaxVelocity, as well as MaxForce, are caps to the velocity and force respectively. The actual scale is determined by Responsiveness.

kid.simple: AlignPosition moves a part to a goal spot and keeps it there. The goal can be another attachment (TwoAttachment mode) or a position you type in (OneAttachment mode). It only moves the part; it does not turn it. For turning, use AlignOrientation.

Holding an object in front of the player (like picking something up)

terms.force: A push or pull. In Roblox it is measured in Roblox force units (mass x studs per second per second). A bigger number is a harder push.
terms.mass: How much 'stuff' an object has, which decides how hard it is to push. A part's mass = its volume x its material density. A 4x1x2 Plastic part (volume 8, density 0.7) has mass 5.6.
terms.gravity: The pull that makes things fall. In Roblox it is `workspace.Gravity`, which is 196.2 studs per second per second by default.
terms.velocity: Speed plus direction, written as a Vector3 in studs per second. Vector3.new(0, 0, 20) means 20 studs every second along the Z direction.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) bundled together. Used for positions, directions, forces and speeds. Y is up.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.center of mass: The balance point of an object. Pushing exactly through it moves the object without spinning it; pushing off to the side also makes it spin.
terms.world space: Directions measured using the whole game world's fixed arrows: Y is always straight up toward the sky, no matter how a part is turned.
terms.attachment space: Directions measured using an attachment's own arrows. If the part tips over, 'up' for the attachment tips over too.
terms.MaxForce: A cap (upper limit) on how hard a constraint is allowed to push. It is a limit, not the amount it always pushes.
terms.Responsiveness: How quickly an Align constraint tries to reach its goal, from 5 (slow and gentle) to 200 (fast and snappy).
terms.magnitude: The length (size) of a vector, ignoring its direction. The magnitude of Vector3.new(3, 4, 0) is 5.
terms.torque: A twisting push that makes things spin, like turning a doorknob or a steering wheel. Torque = force x distance from the spinning point, so pushing farther from the center twists harder.
terms.MaxVelocity: The top speed (studs per second) the part is allowed to move while heading to its goal.
terms.rigidity: With RigidityEnabled, the physics engine snaps to the goal as fast and hard as it can, ignoring MaxForce, MaxVelocity and Responsiveness.
terms.per-axis limit: A separate force cap for each direction (X, Y, Z) instead of one cap for the total.

examples.title: A floating part that glides to a spot
examples.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 2)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Anchored = false
part.Parent = workspace

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

local align = Instance.new("AlignPosition")
align.Attachment0 = attachment
align.Mode = Enum.PositionAlignmentMode.OneAttachment -- use Position, not Attachment1
align.Position = Vector3.new(20, 15, 0)  -- the goal spot in the world
align.Responsiveness = 10                -- fairly gentle (5 = slow, 200 = very snappy)
align.MaxForce = 100000                  -- strong enough to beat gravity
align.MaxVelocity = 30                   -- never faster than 30 studs/s
align.Parent = part

task.wait(3)
align.Position = Vector3.new(-20, 15, 0) -- now glide to a new spot
explain: OneAttachment mode means the goal is the Position value, not another attachment.
The part starts at (0, 10, 0) and glides toward (20, 15, 0). After 3 seconds we change the goal and it glides to (-20, 15, 0).
MaxForce must be bigger than the part's weight (mass x 196.2, about 1098.7 here) or it will sag below the goal.
Responsiveness 10 makes it ease in smoothly; 200 would make it zip there almost instantly.

examples.title: A pet ball that follows a player
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(character)
		local root = character:WaitForChild("HumanoidRootPart")

		-- Goal point: 3 studs right and 2 up from the player's middle
		local goal = Instance.new("Attachment")
		goal.Position = Vector3.new(3, 2, 0)
		goal.Parent = root

		local pet = Instance.new("Part")
		pet.Shape = Enum.PartType.Ball
		pet.Size = Vector3.new(1, 1, 1)
		pet.CanCollide = false
		pet.Massless = true
		pet.Position = root.Position
		pet.Parent = character

		local petAttachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
		petAttachment.Parent = pet

		local follow = Instance.new("AlignPosition")
		follow.Attachment0 = petAttachment -- the pet moves...
		follow.Attachment1 = goal          -- ...to this point next to the player
		follow.Responsiveness = 25
		follow.MaxForce = 10000
		follow.Parent = pet
	end)
end)
explain: The goal attachment is inside the player's HumanoidRootPart. Its Position (3, 2, 0) is measured from the root part's center using the root part's own directions, so the goal is always 3 studs to the player's right and 2 up, even when they turn.
In the default TwoAttachment mode, the pet's Attachment0 is pulled toward Attachment1.
ReactionForceEnabled is off by default, so the pet never tugs on the player.

gotchas: If the part sags below the goal, MaxForce is too small to beat gravity. It must be more than mass x 196.2.
Position is ignored unless Mode is OneAttachment. Attachment1 is ignored when Mode is OneAttachment.
AlignPosition does not turn the part. Add AlignOrientation if it should also face a direction.
If the force is applied off-center the part may tumble. Turn on ApplyAtCenterOfMass.

m.d:
This server-only method returns coarse segment buckets for a player in the current experience. Use these buckets at runtime to personalize content or gate features for specific player groups. If a cached result is not already available, the method may yield while the engine fetches the segment data. Successfully fetched results are cached per player for the lifetime of the server session.

If segment data is unavailable, this method does not throw. Instead, it returns HasData = false and all enum fields are set to Unknown.

This method throws only when called from the client or when the player argument is invalid.

The returned dictionary has the following structure:

Name Type Description
HasData bool Whether segment data was successfully retrieved for the player.
ActivePayerStatus Enum.ActivePayerStatus The player's current payer status bucket for this experience.
WhenUserFirstPlayed Enum.WhenUserFirstPlayed When the player first played this experience, represented as a bucket.
PlatformSpenderStatus Enum.PlayerPlatformSpenderStatus The player's platform-wide spender status bucket, including whether the player falls outside the active spender bucket.
ExperienceActivationStatus Enum.ExperienceActivationStatus Whether the player is new, active, lapsed, or reactivated in this experience, based on the last 30 days.
EngagementLevel Enum.EngagementLevel How many days the player played this experience in the last 7 days, represented as a bucket.
PlatformActivationStatus Enum.PlayerPlatformActivationStatus Whether the player is new, active, lapsed, or reactivated on Roblox, based on the last 60 days.
UserNewReturningStatus Enum.UserNewReturningStatus Whether the player is new to this experience or has played it before.
UserAcquisitionSource Enum.UserAcquisitionSource How the player first found this experience.
m.s: Returns coarse player segment buckets for the current experience.

p.s: The player whose segment buckets should be returned.

class/AngularVelocity.d:
The AngularVelocity constraint applies torque on an assembly to maintain a constant angular velocity. Alternatively:

  • If you want to control the amount of torque applied, use a Torque constraint.
  • If you only need initial angular velocity, set the AssemblyAngularVelocity method directly on the assembly.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Relativity

Application of velocity can be controlled through the constraint's RelativeTo property. If set to World, the angular velocity vector is used as is. If set to Attachment1 and the constraint's Attachment1 property is set to another attachment, the angular velocity will be affected by that of the other attachment. Setting RelativeTo to Attachment1 also exposes the ReactionTorqueEnabled property.
class/AngularVelocity.s: Applies torque on an assembly to maintain a constant angular velocity.

m.d: A Vector3 that gives the desired or target angular velocity. This vector is set in the CFrame expressed by the RelativeTo property.
m.s: A `Datatype.Vector3` that gives the desired or target angular velocity.

kid.simple: The target spin, as a Vector3 in radians per second. The direction is the spin axis and the length is the speed. (0, 3.14, 0) is half a turn per second around Y.
kid.example:
local spin = workspace.Fan.AngularVelocity
spin.AngularVelocity = Vector3.new(0, math.rad(180), 0) -- 180 degrees per second

m.d: Magnitude of the maximum torque the constraint can apply.
m.s: Magnitude of the maximum torque the constraint can apply.

kid.simple: The most twisting strength the constraint is allowed to use to reach the target spin.
kid.example: workspace.Fan.AngularVelocity.MaxTorque = 100000

m.d:
This property, when enabled, causes the constraint to apply equal and opposite reaction forces. This is important if the two attached parts can collide, since without reaction forces collisions can create energy that would otherwise be disregarded.

When enabled, the reaction forces cause the constraint to act like an angular motor between the two attachments.

Only meaningful when RelativeTo is set to Attachment1.
m.s: Causes the constraint to apply equal and opposite reaction forces.

kid.simple: Only matters when RelativeTo is Attachment1. If true, the other part gets twisted the opposite way too, so the constraint acts like a motor between the two parts. This is important if the two parts can bump into each other.
kid.example:
local spin = workspace.Drill.AngularVelocity
spin.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.Attachment1
spin.ReactionTorqueEnabled = true

m.d:
The coordinate frame in which the AngularVelocity vector is expressed, selected by an ActuatorRelativeTo value. If set to World, the angular velocity vector is used as is. If set to Attachment1, the angular velocity is transformed by the CFrame of the assigned attachment.

RelativeTo can also be set to Attachment0, but it makes no physical sense and will lead to unpredictable behaviors.
m.s: The `Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo` value specifying the coordinate frame in which the `Class.AngularVelocity.AngularVelocity|AngularVelocity` vector is expressed; defaults to `Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo|World`.

kid.simple: Picks whose directions the spin uses. World (default): the vector is used as-is in game directions. Attachment1: the spin is measured compared to the other attachment, so if that part turns, the target turns with it. Attachment0 is allowed but behaves unpredictably.
kid.example: workspace.Fan.AngularVelocity.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
kid.gotcha: Avoid Attachment0 here; the docs say it makes no physical sense.

kid.simple: AngularVelocity makes a part spin at a steady speed that you choose. It twists just enough (up to MaxTorque) to keep the spin speed exactly where you set it. Spin speed is measured in radians per second, where about 6.28 is one full turn every second.
kid.analogy: AngularVelocity is like a record player or a ceiling fan set to one speed. It keeps the same spin no matter what, unless something is too heavy for its motor.
whenToUse: Spinning coins, fans and windmills
Spinning obstacles in an obby
Wheels that should turn at a fixed rate
kid.where: Create with Instance.new("AngularVelocity"), set Attachment0 to an attachment in the part to spin, and put it in workspace. Usually from a Script on the server.

terms.angular velocity: How fast something spins, and around which axis, measured in radians per second. 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians per second is one full turn every second.
terms.radians: Another way to measure angles. A full circle is 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians, which is 360 degrees. `math.rad(90)` turns 90 degrees into radians.
terms.torque: A twisting push that makes things spin, like turning a doorknob or a steering wheel. Torque = force x distance from the spinning point, so pushing farther from the center twists harder.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) bundled together. Used for positions, directions, forces and speeds. Y is up.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.assembly: A group of parts that are rigidly joined (for example by welds) so they move as one solid object. A force on any part moves the whole group.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.world space: Directions measured using the whole game world's fixed arrows: Y is always straight up toward the sky, no matter how a part is turned.
terms.attachment space: Directions measured using an attachment's own arrows. If the part tips over, 'up' for the attachment tips over too.
terms.RelativeTo: Chooses whose arrows the numbers use: World (the game world's fixed directions) or Attachment0/Attachment1 (that attachment's own directions, which turn when the part turns).
terms.magnitude: The length (size) of a vector, ignoring its direction. The magnitude of Vector3.new(3, 4, 0) is 5.
terms.MaxTorque: The most twisting force the constraint may use. Too small and a heavy part will spin slower than you asked, or not at all.
terms.reaction torque: The 'twist back'. When one part is spun, the other part gets twisted the opposite way, like a motor between two objects.

examples.title: A spinning obstacle that turns once per second
examples.place: Script inside an unanchored Part (keep it in place with a HingeConstraint or BallSocket to an anchored part)
examples.code:
local part = script.Parent

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

local spin = Instance.new("AngularVelocity")
spin.Attachment0 = attachment
spin.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
-- One full turn per second around the up (Y) axis: 2 x pi radians/s
spin.AngularVelocity = Vector3.new(0, math.pi * 2, 0)
spin.MaxTorque = math.huge -- strong enough for any part
spin.Parent = part
explain: math.pi * 2 is about 6.28 radians, which is one full circle. Per second, that is one turn every second.
The Y in the vector means 'spin around the up-down line', like a merry-go-round.
MaxTorque = math.huge lets it twist as hard as needed to keep that speed, even when players bump into it.

gotchas: The speed is in radians per second, not degrees and not turns. Use math.rad(degrees) to convert, or math.pi * 2 for one turn per second.
If MaxTorque is too small, heavy parts spin slowly or not at all.
AngularVelocity only controls spin, not position. A loose part will still fall; pin it with a hinge or another constraint.
Setting RelativeTo to Attachment0 makes no physical sense and gives strange results. Use World or Attachment1.

class/Animation.d:
An object that references an animation asset (AnimationId) which can be loaded by an AnimationController.

Loading an Animation on Client or Server

In order for AnimationTracks to replicate correctly, it's important to know when they should be loaded on the client or on the server:

  • If an Animator is a descendant of a Humanoid or AnimationController in a player's Player.Character, animations started on that player's client will be replicated to the server and other clients.

  • If the Animator is not a descendant of a player character, its animations must be loaded and started on the server to replicate.

The Animator object must be initially created on the server and replicated to clients for animation replication to work at all. If an Animator is created locally, then AnimationTracks loaded with that Animator will not replicate.

See also Animation Editor and Using Animations to learn how to create and add pre-built or custom animations to your game.
class/Animation.s: References an animation asset which can be loaded by an `Class.AnimationController`.

m.d:
The Content-typed reference to the animation asset for this Animation. It is the underlying storage for AnimationId and accepts animation asset URIs; setting either property updates the other.

Requires Animation security and is not accessible from regular scripts. For most use cases, use AnimationId instead, which provides unrestricted access to the same animation reference as a string content ID.

kid.simple: Another way to store the same animation reference, as a Content value. Changing it changes AnimationId too. Normal scripts should just use AnimationId.

m.d:
This property is the asset ID of the animation an Animation object is referencing. Once an animation has been created and uploaded to Roblox, the ID can be copied from the Creator Dashboard.

Note that the animation will need to be loaded onto an AnimationTrack in order to play it.

kid.example:

animation.AnimationId = "rbxassetid://507770239"

kid.simple: An Animation object just stores the ID of an animation saved on Roblox. It can't play by itself. You load it onto an Animator to get an AnimationTrack, and that track plays it.
kid.analogy: An Animation is like a sticky note with a song's name on it. You need to hand it to a music player (the Animator) to actually hear the song.
whenToUse: Point to an animation you want a character or NPC to play.
Replace one of the default animations (inside the character's Animate script).
kid.where: Make one with `Instance.new("Animation")`, or insert one in Studio (for example inside a script or tool) and paste the ID into AnimationId. Works on the server and the client.

terms.animation: A recorded set of body movements, like a wave or a dance, saved on Roblox with an ID number.
terms.Animation (object): A small object that just holds an animation's ID. It doesn't play anything by itself.
terms.Animator: The object inside a Humanoid (or AnimationController) that actually plays animations on a character.
terms.AnimationTrack: The 'remote control' for one loaded animation. You get it from Animator:LoadAnimation and call Play and Stop on it.
terms.asset ID: The number that identifies something uploaded to Roblox. Animations use it like `rbxassetid://507770239`.
terms.rig: A model set up with joints so it can be animated, like a character.
terms.keyframe: A saved pose at a certain moment in an animation. The animation smoothly moves between keyframes.
terms.fade time: How many seconds an animation takes to smoothly blend in or out, instead of snapping.
terms.weight: How strongly an animation affects the body, from 0 (not at all) to 1 (fully). Used when mixing animations.
terms.priority: Which animation wins when two want to move the same body part. Higher priority (like Action) beats lower (like Idle).
terms.replicate: Copy across the internet so the server and other players see it too.
terms.client: The player's own device. LocalScripts run there.
terms.server: The Roblox computer that runs the game for everyone.

examples.title: Play a wave animation when you press E
examples.code:
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")

local character = script.Parent
local humanoid = character:WaitForChild("Humanoid")
local animator = humanoid:WaitForChild("Animator")

-- 1. Make an Animation object that points to the animation's ID
local waveAnimation = Instance.new("Animation")
waveAnimation.AnimationId = "rbxassetid://507770239" -- Roblox's default R15 wave

-- 2. Load it onto the Animator ONCE to get a track (a remote control)
local waveTrack = animator:LoadAnimation(waveAnimation)
waveTrack.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action -- beat walking/idle animations

-- 3. Play it whenever E is pressed
UserInputService.InputBegan:Connect(function(input, typing)
    if typing then
        return -- ignore keys pressed while typing in chat
    end
    if input.KeyCode == Enum.KeyCode.E and not waveTrack.IsPlaying then
        waveTrack:Play()
    end
end)

waveTrack.Stopped:Connect(function()
    print("Done waving")
end)
explain: Three pieces work together: an Animation (holds the ID) -> the Animator (plays it) -> an AnimationTrack (controls it).
Because this script is in StarterCharacterScripts, it is copied into the character each spawn, so script.Parent is the character.
We call LoadAnimation once and reuse the track. Loading again every time would make lots of extra tracks.
Priority Action makes the wave show over the normal walking and idle animations.
Animations a player plays on their own character from a LocalScript are copied to the server and everyone else automatically.
You can only play animations you or your group own (or Roblox's own), otherwise they won't load.

gotchas: AnimationId must be the full form, like "rbxassetid://507770239", not just the number.
An animation only loads in your game if you (or your group) own it, or Roblox made it.
Animations made for R15 won't look right on R6 characters, and the other way around.
For animations to show for everyone, the Animator should be made on the server (players' characters already have one).

The non-creatable AnimationClip instance type represents abstract animation data that can be fed to the Roblox animation system. KeyframeSequence and CurveAnimation are two current instance types that inherit from AnimationClip.

There are different ways to represent animation data. To simplify the use of Roblox's animation system, all such representations are their own instance types but inherit from the AnimationClip instance. Animation clips published to Roblox via the Animation Editor can be loaded into the Roblox Engine using an Animation instance.
